slides.kicker: It is 2 a.m. Not tired. Wired.
slides.title:
Why can't I just
[[go to sleep]]
like everyone else?
slides.sub: You are not bad at sleep. Your clock runs late.

slides.title:
Your body clock
[[runs late]],
and always has
slides.body: Many ADHD brains send the sleepy signal an hour or two after everyone else's. Midnight to you is ten o'clock to them. That is timing, not stubbornness.

slides.title:
The night is the
first hour that
is [[yours]]
slides.body: All day you were interrupted, managed, needed. Then the house goes quiet and the day finally feels like your own. Of course you do not want to hand it back.

slides.title:
Lights off is
when the [[thoughts]]
clock in
slides.body: Nothing to look at, nothing to do, and every unfinished thing from the day arrives at once. A racing mind at bedtime is a brain with no input.

slides.title:
Anchor the
[[morning]], not
the bedtime
slides.body: A bedtime is a rule you will argue with at 1 a.m. A wake time is a clock you set once. Same time every day, weekends too, and the night slowly follows.

slides.title:
Set an alarm to
[[start]] winding
down, not to sleep
slides.body: You do not notice tired until it is 3 a.m., so make the signal external. An alarm at 10:30 does not mean lights out. It means the next thing you open is the last.

slides.title:
Empty your head
[[before]] the
pillow does it
slides.body: Write down what you would otherwise rehearse in the dark. Tomorrow's first task, the reply you owe, the thing you forgot. On paper, it is not yours to hold.

slides.title:
Put the phone
somewhere you
[[have to walk]]
slides.body: Not face down. Not on charge by the bed. Another room. The scroll is not a habit you break with willpower at midnight. You just make it further away.

slides.title:
Save this for
tonight, around
[[1 a.m.]]
slides.body: You are not broken at sleep. You are running late on a clock nobody set with you. Dump tomorrow into my.adhd before bed, and let the pillow hold nothing.
